title: One microphone, several singers
allegory: A polysemantic neuron is one microphone in a choir recorded with fewer microphones than singers: every mic picks up a blend of voices, so listening to one mic you hear unrelated singers at once.
map: a feature: a direction in activation space
a neuron: one coordinate of the activation
one mic picking up several unrelated singers
superposition: more features than dimensions, the proposed cause
un-mixing all the tracks into single voices
a sparse autoencoder recovering feature directions

cap.1: Say you read what makes one neuron fire: cooking recipes, and also legal contracts. Nothing links them. Reading neurons one at a time stops working.
cap.2: A polysemantic neuron fires for several unrelated things, so 'what does this neuron do?' has no single answer and neuron-by-neuron interpretation breaks down.
cap.3: Polysemanticity is an observation about a basis direction: its activating inputs fall into several unrelated clusters, defeating a one-neuron-one-concept reading.

cap.1: Picture a choir recorded with fewer microphones than singers. Each mic picks up a blend of voices, so one mic's track has a soprano and a bass in it.
cap.2: Each feature is a direction spread across many neurons, and each neuron adds up bits of many features. With more features than neurons, blends are unavoidable.
cap.3: A neuron's activation sums the active features' projections onto its axis. If features outnumber dimensions they cannot all be axis-aligned: that is superposition.

chapters.name: Two ways to blend
chapters.verdict: Polysemanticity is the symptom. Superposition is one proposed cause, not a synonym.

cap.1: Mics blend voices for two reasons: they sit at angles between singers, or there are simply more singers than mics. Same symptom, different causes.
cap.2: A neuron can be polysemantic because features just don't line up with neurons, or because the layer stores more features than it has neurons. Only the second is superposition.
cap.3: Leading view: superposition, favoured by sparsity. But a non-privileged basis, a mislabelled single feature or a mid-computation neuron can also look polysemantic. Test before naming it.

cap.1: Singers who seldom sing at the same time can share mics cheaply. The blend only hurts when two sing at once, which gets rare fast as each sings less.
cap.2: If each feature is active with chance p, two given features collide with chance p². As p shrinks, collisions fall much faster than usefulness, so packing pays.
cap.3: Interference cost scales with co-occurrence (p² for independent features), which falls faster than p. Sparsity tips the trade: dense data gives PCA, sparse data gives superposition.

cap.1: To hear single voices, un-mix all the tracks together. With a big enough desk you can pull out each singer from few mics, as long as few sing at once.
cap.2: A sparse autoencoder learns many more directions than there are neurons and rebuilds each activation from just a few of them. Those directions tend to mean one thing each.
cap.3: SAEs (dictionary learning) exploit sparsity: an overcomplete dictionary under a sparsity penalty recovers candidate monosemantic latents from polysemantic neurons.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Don't read neurons one at a time

cap.1: A neuron that seems to mean two unrelated things is expected, not a mistake in your reading. The meaningful units usually spread across many neurons.
cap.2: Polysemanticity is why interpretability moved from single neurons to directions and SAE latents. Expect it wherever a layer must hold more concepts than it has neurons.
cap.3: Understanding or steering a model needs units that mean one thing. Polysemantic neurons are not those units, which is the case for feature directions, SAEs and probes.

readouts.f: b2 > 0 && b2 != a ? 'singers ' + min(a, b2) + ' and ' + max(a, b2) : 'singer ' + a

caption.1: One singer alone is heard cleanly, though both mics carry them. Add singer 3 alongside singer 1: the reader hears singer 2, who is silent. Try the threshold.
caption.2: Five feature directions in a two-neuron space. One active feature decodes cleanly because cross-talk stays under the threshold; two at once and the wrong voice comes through.
caption.3: Decoder ReLU(w_k·h − b) over 5 pentagon directions in 2-D: single-feature cross-talk (cos 72° ≈ 0.31) is cut by b, but co-activation breaks it. Sparsity keeps that rare.

where_else: Sparse autoencoders and transcoders, built to un-mix polysemantic activations
The cocktail party problem: separating many voices from a few microphones
Compressed sensing: recovering a sparse signal from fewer measurements than unknowns

hamming.what: One neuron firing for several unrelated things, so a single neuron is not a single concept.
hamming.when: Whenever you read a model neuron by neuron, especially in layers that must hold many more concepts than they have neurons.
hamming.why: It is why interpretability works with directions and dictionary features instead of individual neurons.

object.title: The microphone stand
object.subtitle: Three mics as axes, four singers as arrows; no singer stands on an axis.

plane.label: mic 1 is loud on this side

cap.1: Three mics are the three axes; four singers are the four arrows. None of the singers stands on an axis.
cap.2: A three-neuron layer holding four features as directions, none aligned with a neuron.
cap.3: Four feature directions in a 3-D activation space arranged as a tetrahedron, one of the shapes the toy models of superposition produce.

cap.1: The sheet marks where mic 1 is loud. Singers A and B are both on the loud side, so mic 1 fires for both of them.
cap.2: Neuron 1 is positive for features A and B: a polysemantic neuron, from geometry alone.
cap.3: A neuron's pre-activation is the projection onto its axis, so every feature with a positive component along it drives it.

cap.1: Look along another mic and it fires for a different pair. Every mic is a blend; no mic is one singer.
cap.2: Each axis splits the four features two and two, so every neuron responds to two unrelated features.
cap.3: No coordinate axis isolates a single feature; the monosemantic units are the directions, not the basis vectors.

cap.1: Four singers, three mics: they cannot all get an axis of their own. That squeeze is superposition, the leading explanation for blended neurons.
cap.2: More features than dimensions forces overlap. The model accepts the interference because sparse features seldom fire together.
cap.3: With n features in d < n dimensions, directions cannot be orthogonal; the model trades interference for capacity, which pays off under sparsity.

cap.1: A sparse autoencoder would learn one arrow per singer, pointing straight at each cluster, instead of listening mic by mic.
cap.2: An SAE's dictionary directions aim at the feature arrows, not at the axes, which is why its latents read more cleanly than neurons.
cap.3: Dictionary learning recovers the feature directions as an overcomplete basis; interpretability then works in that basis rather than the neuron basis.

predict.q: Four features live in a three-neuron layer. Can every feature have a neuron of its own?

options.t: No: at least two must overlap, so some neurons blend
Yes, if training runs long enough

predict.why: Four directions cannot all sit on three axes. That forced overlap is superposition.

predict.q: When does packing extra features in cost the model least?

options.t: When features are rarely active at the same time
When every feature is active on every input

predict.why: Overlap only hurts when two features fire together. With dense data the toy model gives up and behaves like PCA.

predict.q: Is polysemanticity the same thing as superposition?

options.t: No: it is the symptom, and superposition is one proposed cause
Yes: the two words mean the same thing

predict.why: A neuron can also blend features because nothing makes features line up with neurons, with no superposition at all.

object.where: Anywhere few sensors record many sparse sources: microphones and voices, compressed sensing, neurons and features.
